draft.title: Statutes that protect rights
card: A statute is a law made by parliament. Australia has no national bill of rights, so many rights are protected by statutes that cover particular areas.
a Commonwealth law that makes it unlawful to treat people unfairly because of their race, colour, descent or national or ethnic origin.
a Commonwealth law that makes it unlawful to treat people unfairly because of their sex, marital status, pregnancy or family responsibilities, and it also covers sexual harassment.

Each statute protects rights only in the areas it covers, such as work, education and the provision of goods and services. A person with a complaint must show that their situation falls within the Act.
draft.remember: Statutes protect rights one area at a time, not through a single general guarantee.

a.q: Why are statutes such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 described as protecting rights in particular areas?
opts: Each Act covers set grounds and areas of life
Each Act applies only in one State or Territory
Each Act can be overridden by any other statute
Each Act protects every right a person has
a.why: These Acts name the grounds, such as race or sex, and the areas, such as work or education, where discrimination is unlawful. They do not protect every right, and they are Commonwealth laws, so they are not limited to one State.
a.clue: Think about what each Act lists as its grounds and areas.

b.q: Dana is refused a job at a Newcastle warehouse because the manager says she is a woman and 'will have children soon'. Which law most directly protects her?
opts: The Sex Discrimination Act 1984
The Racial Discrimination Act 1975
The right to trial by jury
A national bill of rights
b.why: The treatment is based on Dana's sex and family responsibilities, which the Sex Discrimination Act covers in employment. The Racial Discrimination Act is tempting because it is also an anti-discrimination law, but the ground here is not race. Australia has no national bill of rights.
b.clue: Match the ground of the unfair treatment to the Act.

a.best: Each Act covers set grounds and areas of life

problems.detail: The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 grounds are given as a complete list: sex, marital status, pregnancy or family responsibilities. The Act also covers potential pregnancy, breastfeeding, relationship status and, since 2013, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status. The list is out of date unless it is marked as examples, for instance with 'such as'.

The why says the treatment is based on 'family responsibilities'. Under the Act, family responsibilities means caring for existing dependants. 'Will have children soon' fits sex and potential pregnancy, which the card does not list. Students are left matching the scenario to a ground that does not strictly apply.

check.summary: The card's list of Sex Discrimination Act grounds is incomplete and out of date: it leaves out sexual orientation, gender identity, intersex status, breastfeeding and potential pregnancy. Question b's why wrongly names family responsibilities as the ground when the scenario is about sex and potential pregnancy. Both answers are otherwise sound.
